newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury 3-yr note auction disappoints market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury 3-yr note auction disappoints market.

text.p: The Treasury's auction of $17.0 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday disappointed the market, attracting less bidding interest than had been hoped for, analysts said.
"The market was sure of a solid auction so the average results and poor bid-to-cover ratio left some disappointment," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
The Treasury sold the three-year notes at an average yield of 6.438 percent with a stop of 6.449 percent, a "tail" of 1.1 basis points.

The value of bids submitted over those accepted, the bid-to-cover ratio, was 2.08, lower than the 2.30 average bid-to-cover ratio for the four three-year auctions in 1996 and the last one, in February.

"The statistics were distinctly on the soft side," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi. "The bid to cover was low at 2.08 and people were only bidding for $17.0 billion in three-year notes so the bid to cover ratio should have been a little higher."
The 1.1 basis point tail was the widest for a three-year sale since Aug. 8, 1995 when it was 2.2 basis points, he said.

"The three-year note was disappointing, no doubt about it," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds. "The bid-to-cover ratio was well below average."
Flanagan said an uptick in the value of noncompetitive bids to $967 million "had to do with the 6-3/8 percent coupon, the best level in about a year."
Flanagan said investors decided that the market had become "very expensive" and was not making enough allowance for the possibility of another Federal Reserve interest rate increase.
"We were overbought; we were expensive," said Flanagan.
"The market doesn't look cheap at all unless you think the Fed is out of the picture -- and I don't," said Stiles.
Stiles said the only positive feature of the auction was the $967 million in non-competitive bids.
"It doesn't seem that investors are excited enough about current price levels to chase the market," he said.
Stiles said the sale of $12.0 billion in 10-year Treasury notes on Wednesday could benefit from a speculative play.
"People might be hoping to buy the 10-years here and sell at higher prices after the (April) retail sales report next week," he said.

"I'm not sure what this three-year auction means for 10-years," said Flanagan. "They're two entirely different animals. You have to believe that the curve has become very expensive which leads you to believe that there isn't much more room for progress."
But if prices go lower and yields rise, that might spur interest in Wednesday's bidding for the 10-years, he said.
Rupkey said the low bid-to-cover in the three-year note auction signified that retail investors were not as interested in the auction as people had thought.

But he said if one wanted to put a positive spin on that minimal interest, one could reason that people want to lengthen the average maturity of their portfolios by buying the 10-year notes in the Treasury auction on Wednesday.
"If you want to lengthen your durations, you don't buy three-years; you buy 10-years," said Rupkey.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679))
